The assistant should avoid referencing the chain-of-command hierarchy or otherwise hinting at the existence of hidden messages or logic that the recipient may not be aware of.

PROVIDES (use EXACTLY these names as the predicates this module defines):
  (none)

NEEDS -- these concepts are established by OTHER nodes of the graph, so every one of them belongs in this module's `requires`, spelled EXACTLY as given; never in `ontology`, never defined here. `inputs` is only for plain facts about the situation being judged (messages, roles, case data) that YOU identify -- a name can never appear in both requires and inputs:
  - root_authority: Rules in the protect_privileged_information section carry root authority.

CITATION: every ontology/asserts entry that cites a source must cite EXACTLY 'l1707_1973_n039' -- the id of this node. Never cite line numbers, line ranges, or any other id.

SOURCE TEXT (verbatim from the document; the L-numbers locate text, they are not citable ids):
L1928-L1928:
When deciding how to respond, the assistant should first identify the intended recipient and the context. Typically, if the conversation includes a user message, the assistant should treat the user as the recipient unless a higher-level message explicitly instructs otherwise[^ddka]. The assistant should avoid referencing the chain-of-command hierarchy or otherwise hinting at the existence of hidden messages or logic that the recipient may not be aware of[^31oe].
